chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Other near-miss hits: 'Hot and Anxious' and the riff that became 'Castle Rock'
summary: At Chicago's Circle Inn, Al Sears' men paid $5 requests for Horace's riff while writing it down, and it appeared on record as 'Castle Rock'.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: But I've had some near misses on hits, man, you know.

I wrote another tune called 'Hot and Anxious,' and this was taken away with some more riffs. I wrote another thing with a guy listening at me play it in Chicago at a club called the Circle Inn. We didn't have the thing named or anything. It was a riff, one of those things. And that tune became a hit, and I'm going to recall the name of this tune because I want a few people who might hear this to remember it. I had the hit taken away from this particular tune. And you'll remember this. You remember a tune -- called 'Castle Rock?'
We were playing this with my five piece group, and this was the riff. There's a guy named Al Sears. I think he was a tenor player, and he was with --

-- Duke for quite a spell, and then Johnny Hodges had a small group at one time, you know, and I think -- I don't know if he was in that group or not, but I know he was with Duke. Well, here's what happened. We were playing this thing at 6030 Cottage Grove in a little club called Circle Inn right next to the elevator, and Al Sears and three or four of his musicians came in one night, and we were playing this riff, and, man, they liked it. They sat at the bar -- on top of the bar. You know how that is, where the band was playing. We had to go inside the bar (unintelligible) the bandstand. And the band was sitting all
around. So after we'd played this tune once, we had a request with a $5.00 bill to play that same tune again.

This is exactly what happened. So it became obvious, and we played it the second time. They sent up another $5.00. We said, 'What's happening,' and so we happened to look down. There were two guys, and they was writing (illegible), you know, one of those things. And that's how 'Castle Rock' started. And a few months later here's a recording came out of 'Castle Rock,' one of those things, and my saxophone player came to work one night and he says, 'Man, I heard our riff. They've called it 'Castle Rock' and Al Sears or so and so recorded it and all.' There it was. So that got away.
So he made some money off of that tune too. So -- I mean quite a bit. That tune got real popular, you know. So that was that.
